speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will allow Members to raise questions or express their views on both Bills during the debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We will still have the formal Second Reading of the Active Mobility Bill to ensure that procedural requirements are dealt with.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: First, I would like to thank our delivery riders, who have been instrumental in providing delivery services to Singaporeans during this COVID-19 circuit breaker period.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is not an easy job; they brave the elements and are on the move all day.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I am grateful for their efforts in making our lives more convenient, amidst this trying time for all of us.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In many cities around the world, we have seen an uptake in active mobility modes of transport after the outbreak of COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have observed a similar trend in Singapore, where travel demand for active mobility devices appears to have increased, even as ridership for public transport, taxis and private hire cars fell drastically.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This has arisen because of the larger number of short trips between homes and neighbourhood centres.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With the expansion of the cycling path network in the years ahead, we should also expect use of active mobility devices to pick up again.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With more users, it is all the more critical for us to strengthen our regulations and enforcement even as we deal with other COVID-related challenges.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Active Mobility Bill allows LTA to shorten the forfeiture process for such devices which pose significant safety risks, and expands the public path network to include certain open spaces, so that active mobility devices can be used safely in accordance to our regulations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Today, only active mobility devices that comply with device criteria on weight, width and speed are allowed to be used on public paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is to enhance public safety on paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Motorised PMDs and PABs are also required to meet the relevant safety standards, which is the UL2272 standard for motorised PMDs and the European Standard EN15194 for PABs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have introduced many measures to tackle the supply of non-compliant devices, including prohibiting the sale of non-UL2272 devices for use on public paths since July 2019 and mandating inspection of e-scooters from April 2020.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA regularly enforces against retailers who display, advertise and sell non-compliant devices, and alter devices to make them non-compliant, as well as path users who ride such non-compliant devices on public paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Despite our efforts, LTA continues to detect non-compliant devices being used on public paths, and fires involving non-compliant devices continue to occur.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In 2019, 11 retailers were caught for displaying non-compliant PMDs and PABs and failing to display warning notices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In view of these challenges, we need to go upstream to stem the inflow of non-compliant devices at the point of import.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For a start, we will implement this requirement for motorised PMDs and PABs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will ensure that we have oversight of the inflow into Singapore of all such devices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA will assess import approval applications based on the safety of the devices to be imported.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It will be an offence to import motorised PMDs and PABs without valid approval from LTA.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We recognise that there are legitimate reasons to import non-compliant devices, such as for research, re-export or commercial use exclusively on private land or land with restricted public access.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA will also affix tamper-proof tags on all non-compliant devices allowed to be imported, to facilitate downstream enforcement.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will take decisive enforcement against the provision of false information and imports without import approvals.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Similar to other import controls regimes, ICA officers appointed as officers of customs will work with LTA to carry out random inspections at the checkpoints.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA is also empowered to conduct searches of premises or conveyances located within any premises, used for or in connection with the import of small motorised vehicles or the storage of such imported vehicles, in order to investigate an offence under the Bill.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This could include premises suspected to contain motorised PMDs and PABs imported without valid import approval from LTA.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Motorised PMDs and PABs found to be imported without valid import approval will be seized and forfeited and their importers will be taken to task.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Non-compliant devices pose fire risks even when not being used or charged.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since the Active Mobility Act (AMA) was passed by this House in 2017, LTA has seized PMDs, PABs and bicycles used in the commission of offences under the AMA or the Road Traffic Act (RTA) and stores these in holding yards pending the outcome of prosecution or the acceptance of a composition offer.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Some are not UL2272 or EN15194 compliant and others could have been badly damaged or have leaking batteries after being involved in accidents.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It would be dangerous for LTA to retain custody of such forfeited devices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There will be no changes to the forfeiture and disposal process for non-compliant devices that are not dangerous.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition to PMDs, PABs and bicycles, the process also extends to non-compliant mobility vehicles, or what we refer to as personal mobility aids.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Path-connected open spaces are generally indistinguishable from the existing public path network.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This includes spaces such as courtyards, plazas, squares and atriums that are accessible to the public.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This amendment will allow our public path network to accommodate the largest range of possible users.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It will also enable LTA to extend the public path user rules to reduce potential conflicts between the motorised and non-motorised users in these open spaces.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The clarity will be useful to all path users.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We understand that some of these path-connected open spaces are used for community or municipal functions, such as grassroots events, night markets or community roadshows.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will facilitate events and activities by allowing open spaces to be closed temporarily.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This delinks LTA's regulatory and enforcement functions from the associated revenues from these actions and aligns LTA's financial practices with the whole-of-Government financial governance framework.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We remain committed in promoting active mobility as a viable and attractive mode of transport and lifestyle choice in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is timely for us to put in place a regulatory framework to ensure that active mobility devices being brought into and used in Singapore are safe.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is a key step in helping us put in place a safe and sustainable active mobility landscape in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since the Active Mobility Act (AMA) came into force in May 2018, much has been done to strengthen the safe usage of active mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Examples include the introduction of the UL2272 certification and the mandatory registration of active mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I have a few clarifications and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What will be the responsibilities of e-commerce platforms, such as Tao Bao, Qoo10, and Carousell?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the onus on ensuring device compliance be imposed on e-commerce consumers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If onus is indeed placed on consumers, we should strive to raise awareness of compliant active mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would suggest that LTA consider active promotion of compliant models.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having a "white list" of devices that meet the latest regulations would help consumers make better purchase decisions from both physical stores and online platforms.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When it comes to purchasing from online platforms, Members of this House will know that there are instances when an online seller ships a wrong product to the buyer, either deliberately or by mistake.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In an event where a buyer purchases a compliant model, but the online seller ships a non-compliant one to him, would the unknowing buyer be liable for an offence under section 5 of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Remote as it may be, there is a possibility that some may create their own non-compliant active mobility device by piecing together various replacement parts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Already, we have seen instances of PMDs being "souped up" to provide more power, more speed, more battery life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such modifications can be dangerous and I hope that LTA can take proactive steps to deter this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that the cost of obtaining third-party liability insurance is not exorbitant, and more importantly, we need to ensure that victims would be adequately covered for any medical bills arising in the unfortunate event of a PMD-related accident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed import restrictions are a timely measure that will further enhance the safety of our homes and our public paths.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They have, in the midst of a pandemic, risen to the occasion to deliver all manner of goods, so that the majority of the population can stay at home and practise social distancing measures and live their life as normally as is possible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The demand for delivery services is on the rise, and it will continue to stay high even after circuit breaker measures ease, as we navigate this pandemic.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: More people are taking up delivery jobs to supplement their lost income.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As a result, we will see more mobility devices out in public.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some users are also relying on these devices to get out and about for their daily exercise.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With fewer options to spend their free time, I observe that more residents are taking to the parks and park connectors, bringing their devices with them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When the Active Mobility Bill was debated this February, me and several of my Parliamentary colleagues expressed concerns about fire risks with the increased usage of PMDs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just last week, last Wednesday, to be specific, there was a fire in Nee Soon South at 4.30 am.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Luckily, there was no major injury but three occupants were sent to hospital.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is timely that Minister has followed up swiftly with the introduction of upstream measures to prevent the unauthorised import of non-compliant devices which do not meet safety requirements.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The shortening of the current forfeiture process will also help to conserve resources spent on storing impounded devices, as well as mitigate fire safety hazards from storing these devices for prolonged periods.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This would hopefully serve as a strong statement to those who knowingly purchase or import non-compliant devices or refuse to do their due diligence on this matter.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These new measures are indicative of the authorities’ determination to stamp out such devices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Targeting non-compliant imports will help to nip the problem in the bud.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, as some of these devices and their parts may be purchased online by individuals from overseas companies, how does the relevant agency manage these individual imports?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Like the fire that I just mentioned that happened last week, what I understand is that the PMD was new and it was left to charge for the first time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: According to the SCDF report, there is no approval label on the PMD.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, why do people still buy these devices?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps MOT need to study why people still buy non-compliant PMDs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: During the circuit breaker, I also received worrying feedback from residents about e-scooters reappearing on the pedestrian paths.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Due to reduced footfall on the pedestrian paths, some would even speed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Pedestrians still do use the paths, and any number of accidents, especially fatal ones, is one too many.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Whoever these riders are and whatever their reasons, no one is above the law.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They must not ride their PMDs on the pedestrian paths.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How can enforcement be stepped up, especially during manpower constraints and social distancing measures?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are the relevant authorities exploring the use of technology, such as facial recognition or, perhaps even drones, to quicken the process for identifying perpetrators and arresting them?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Previously, I also raised safety concerns for residents waiting at the bus stops and open spaces.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even with the new laws in place, some errant riders would not disembark when they should as they do not want to inconvenience themselves.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Town centres, plazas, courtyards and squares have high pedestrian traffic and are not appropriate for PMDs or PABs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Most riders have been understanding on this matter.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is something that I feel very strongly about.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I had spoken to LTA officers many times on this issue.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Safety is paramount and even with fewer pedestrians out and about, this must not be taken for granted.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As circuit measures ease, the footfalls will be back.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If PMD riders continue their errant ways, I fear that we will see a spate of accidents because they have become used to cruising the pedestrian paths.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the meantime, I urge pedestrians to stay alert and vigilant as you get out and about.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   	In February this year, when we were debating the Active Mobility Bill, several Members of Parliament and I expressed concerns about the fire risks associated with the increased usage of PMDs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Last week, there was a fire caused by a PMD in Nee Soon South and this has made me even more worried about this problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am very pleased to see that the Government has quickly introduced this amendment Bill to tackle the non-compliant PMDs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some PMDs and spare parts can be bought online; may I ask how the Government is going to check these PMDs?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, we have just given our residents some peace of mind not so long ago.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should not reduce all these rules and regulations to nothing but paper tigers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Back in April 2016, at the 2016 Committee of Supply Debates for MOT, I had mentioned that unauthorised e-bikes were still available for sale.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I said that many e-bikes which were in use were not authorised models and I asked the Ministry to consider only allowing authorised e-bikes to be sold in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was when MOT was looking at introducing new active mobility laws and looking to promote use of PMDs for first and last mile connectivity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Less than four years later, on 4 November 2019, on the day MOT announced in Parliament that e-scooters were to be banned from the footpaths, consigning it into, at the least, temporary obsolescence for many users, I had a Parliamentary Question that day asking what are the measures in place to deter the sale and supply of non-compliant PMDs in Singapore by online suppliers and whether the Ministry has asked Singapore Customs to help detect and prevent non-compliant PMDs from being brought into Singapore by any supplier or individual.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I wondered why it has taken so long for the Government to cut this import of illegal e-scooters or e-bikes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The public had to endure wide usage of illegal specs e-scooters and e-bikes for some time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Till today, I still see quite a few illegal e-bikes being used.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister of State Lam also mentioned this recently.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I remember in the debate for the Second Reading of the Active Mobility Bill, I was asking about allowing throttle operated e-bikes and Senior Minister of State Lam gave his explanation as to why throttle e-bikes were not allowed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But till today, we still see throttle e-bikes around.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After the Bill is passed today, the requirement for import approvals will likely be a first step to make sure that we do not have unauthorised e-bikes or e-scooters, and in fact, other types of PMDs, some of which we may not even be able to imagine at this moment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to make sure that the controls are in place to ensure that no unauthorised small motorised vehicles can even be shipped into Singapore via any shipping lines or logistic service providers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They must be stopped at all our customs checkpoints for land, air or sea.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The logistic service providers of all importers including online suppliers must be made aware and accountable for the ban.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Online e-commerce suppliers must not allow sale and import of such unauthorised machines into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will someone who try ordering an illegal vehicle online from a foreign webpage be told before paying and checking out that it cannot be delivered to Singapore?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For instance, a link to these requirements can be placed on a prominent place on the LTA website's landing page.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I now move on to the Active Mobility (Amendment No. 2) Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support this Bill’s intention to extend the coverage of the law to include path-related open spaces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 4 amends section 6(1) to allow for any such space to be declared pedestrian-only, footpath or a shared path by LTA whether be it in public land or private land.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would LTA consult the local stakeholders before declaring any area to be a specific type of path?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also support the Bill’s intentions to enable the earlier disposal by LTA of seized non-compliant active mobility vehicles for safety reason.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: May the Senior Minister of State also share with this House how does LTA currently dispose the seized vehicles?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are they taken apart and sold for scrap locally or abroad?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How are the batteries disposed of, bearing in mind the safety risks associated with illegal batteries?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am a daily user of a popular park near my home as well as a park connector leading up to the East Coast Park and I concur with those reports.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My use of the parks and park connectors during the circuit breaker reinforced my previous views on the culture of foot path or park connector use by all users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even without a large number of e-scooters in use, as we have previously seen, we can do more to improve on the culture – keeping left, giving way, or giving space to each other; riders reducing speed when approaching other users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have previously spoken of how information needs to be piped to those who do not sign up for a course or do not actively seek such information online, including cyclists and device users as well as pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that the MOT and LTA will look at how to enhance the public education efforts for shared use of foot paths and public connectors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I would like to talk about adequate enforcement – the other limb necessary for safe active mobility use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On 5 May, The Straits Times reported that Senior Minister of State Lam had said that there has been increased use of non-compliant personal mobility devices (PMDs) on roads during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even though we have seen fewer e-scooters around, there is hardly a day for me when I do not see any e-scooters on foot paths or on the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are still e-scooters defying the ban after so many months.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These riders clearly think they can get away with it because they do not sense that they will be taken to task immediately.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am really not sure that enforcement is indeed sufficient with spot checks on certain locations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, I use the Siglap Park Connector daily and I have never seen enforcement officers in the vicinity of the connector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unless one pushes his e-scooter to the park connector, most riders will need to ride on the road or on foot paths to get to the park connector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the one along Hougang Avenue 7.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sure I am not the only person who has recently seen e-scooter riders riding across the road at traffic lights.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even if we think that these days, we may not see as many e-scooters as we used to do before the foot path ban, we should not forget that when the expanded cycling path network is up, e-scooters may yet be popular again.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it is important that we get the issues of public education and adequate enforcement right, or we will be kicking the can down the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are mostly from Grab and on two occasions, Foodpanda.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it is not clear as to how those laws were imposed on obligations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So I raised the same concerns again at the Committee of Supply debate for MOT this year and also suggested the imposition of penalties on the food delivery companies in the event of any failure on the part of their riders to comply with the law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister of State Lam said in response and I quote, "Businesses have a role to play, which is why LTA has introduced regulations on companies and continues to work closely with companies to encourage responsible behaviour in their riders." But no further details were given on enforcement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The nagging question I have about the expanded cycling path network is whether cycling paths will be directly linked to HDB blocks, condominiums, houses, shophouses, office buildings and industrial buildings such that riders do not need to alight and push their PMDs or e-bikes along foot paths to their homes, workplaces or other destinations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If riders need to pass a foot path or road en route to their destination, it may result in some e-scooter or e-bike riders continuing riding on the path and taking the easy way out.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As e-bikes have become more commonly seen after the foot path ban for e-scooters, we also see more e-bikes on foot paths now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We may end up kidding ourselves after spending so much money on the expanded cycling path network – that it will solve the problems created by e-scooters' use of foot paths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this seems too expensive, impractical or ambitious, then MOT may need to reconsider e-scooters and other PMDs as a serious option for first and final mile connectivity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, if our cycling path network were to become sufficiently extensive, such that PMD and e-bike riders do not need to alight and push, it may in turn do away with the need for cyclists to share the use of foot paths, which is still currently allowed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This prospect may be welcomed by many foot path users who may not think that sharing foot paths with cyclists is a good idea.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have asked these questions earlier this year and I look forward to the Senior Minister of State's clarification today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also sensible for us to address the fire risk posed by non-compliant active mobility devices held by LTA before any incidents occur.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three clarifications to raise on the Active Mobility (Amendment No. 2) Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point relates to the return of a non-compliant forfeited vehicle that has been deemed dangerous.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even if such a vehicle were not linked to an offence, it seems extremely unsafe to return a vehicle that is too dangerous for LTA to retain to an individual.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify under what circumstances such a vehicle may be returned to the individual?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the safety of the vehicle be a pre-condition for such a return?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point relates to the notice requirement before selling, destroying or disposing of a non-compliant vehicle that is dangerous to retain.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that the e-Gazette was made public earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the reality is that publication in the Gazette will not be a meaningful notification for the average individual.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 53(3A) applies to vehicles that are moved to a holding yard under section 45 or section 46.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both sections require LTA to give notice of the move to the owner of the vehicle as soon as practicable, if the owner is known.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This requirement does not seem to apply where LTA intends to exercise its powers under section 53(3A).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify in a situation where the owner is known, whether LTA will be required to give notice to the owner of its intention to sell, destroy or dispose of potentially dangerous non-compliant vehicle under the new section 53(3A)?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point relates to the risks that continue to be posed by non-compliant vehicles held at the holding yards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The danger is compounded when you consider that there are other vehicles in the holding yards that are similarly dangerous or materially increase the likelihood of an outbreak of fire.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what safety measures are put in place to mitigate the risk of fire at the holding yards?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, in the worst-case scenario that a fire breaks out, who is liable for the damage caused?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, in the event that the fire can be traced back to a single vehicle, would the owner of that vehicle be liable for the damage caused by the fire caused by their vehicle, notwithstanding that the vehicle is now in the custody of LTA?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They filled a transport need that our public transport system and existing private vehicles could not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But as we discovered, this came at a high cost to safety – from accidents on roads and foot paths to charging fires at home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, new regulations will impose a cost on businesses and commuters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We need to minimise these costs while still ensuring that regulations serve the purpose of promoting public safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In some respects, this Bill imposes more regulations on importers of small motorised vehicles than our existing laws on the import of motor vehicles do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, under existing law, any person in Singapore may import a motor vehicle, subject to import approval from Customs and vehicle registration from LTA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The concept of a licence to import motor vehicles simply does not exist under the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our approach for motor vehicles is to regulate the vehicles rather than to regulate the importers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill, in contrast, will create a regulatory regime to license small motorised vehicle importers directly under section 5 of the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Further, the Bill's powers also extend to import of components for small motorised vehicles, which also affects repair services and even individuals who may wish to import spare parts for their own repairs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It will be critical for LTA to implement a robust framework that ensures competition will be maintained while maintaining safety standards for users and the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My concerns range over three areas: who is allowed to import; what small motorised vehicles can be imported; and whether regulations will be made under the Act to cover competition in the market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, I wish to ask how the framework for approving importers will be applied and whether it will facilitate entry and competition in the market for small motorised vehicles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned that consumers may face higher prices and fewer choices if prospective dealers are unable to gain approval or are discouraged by high licensing requirements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, will consumers have a choice to directly import their small motorised vehicles from overseas suppliers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, will overseas sellers be licensed to sell direct to consumers in Singapore or can consumers be licensed to import for private use if the vehicle meets standards?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I wish to clarify the framework for approving small motorised vehicles for import.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore is a small market, manufacturers may be reluctant to design small motorised vehicles to meet Singapore-specific requirements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Will study whether international design standards for small motorised vehicles such as those in force in China are suitable for Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If so, will certifications from the relevant international authorities be acceptable for import purposes?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Or is the intention to develop local certification capability and how quickly and cost effectively can that be done?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A related concern is on the import of small motorised vehicle components.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A broad reading of the Act suggests components could also be subject to import control because these vehicles can be easily assembled from parts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If enforced strictly, this would affect competition in the market for servicing and repairs, and prevent consumers from sourcing their own repair parts from overseas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Will LTA consider limiting import restrictions only to components which are integral to the small motorised vehicle or which are safety critical such as the motor, chassis and batteries?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned that these regulations will reduce the number of firms in the market and hence, enhance market power over consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As we know, similar issues can arise in the motor vehicle market, which is dominated by a small number of firms who are the exclusive authorised dealers for the major car manufacturers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Within car brands, the only competition really comes from parallel importers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the case of the car market, the barrier to entry, they are not just regulatory in nature, they arrive in the combination of the small domestic market, combine manufacturer's decisions to authorise dealers on an exclusive basis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to seek clarification on two areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the Authority's power of forfeiture of vehicles under both Bills; and second, the ambit of the definition of "path-connected open spaces" in the Active Mobility (Amendement No. 2) Bill or AMB, and plans under this Bill to harmonise the use of such spaces amongst pedestrians and vehicle users.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the first issue, I wish to make two points.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, the power of forfeiture is limited to situations where a person has been convicted or compounds an offence in relation to the Active Mobility Act (AMA), or the Road Traffic Act (RTA).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, the Court retains jurisdiction on the issue of forfeiture.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a situation where the Authority orders forfeiture of a non-compliant vehicle posing a hazard, there could be a perceived conflict of interest arising.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because the Authority enforces the AMA and will also enforce the Small Motorised Vehicles Bill (SMVB) once it is enacted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then, the Authority exercises a power of forfeiture of this vehicle, that is subject matter of ongoing criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Let us take an example of a person who was brought to book and charged in Court by the Authority for importing and using a non-compliant PMD.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His PMD has been seized and stored by the Authority.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before it concludes, Authority takes the view that the continued storage of the PMD is dangerous and wants to have it forfeited.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the provision, it can do so at once, without reference to the accused or the Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder whether it would be better to vest with the Court the jurisdiction to deal with such matters instead?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From a policy view point, may I please ask, what is the purpose of providing to the Authority the power to release a non-compliant vehicle used in a commission of an offence back into public circulation?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe the hon Member, Mr Louis Ng, made a similar point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is noteworthy that the Authority, in the same provision, may refer the matter to the Magistrate who must order a forfeiture if he finds that the non-compliant vehicle was used in the commission of an offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, the Magistrate has no discretion and it seems to me that we may be proposing to give the Authority a wider power than the Magistrate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to bear in mind that the purpose behind the SMVB is to dry up the number of non-compliant vehicles in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Minister of State, Dr Lam had already highlighted the fire hazard as well as the big numbers of non-compliant vehicles that were forfeited just last year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Moving on to the second issue, I wish to first deal with the AMB provisions dealing with the extension of the public path system to include path connected open spaces.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This makes eminent sense as it will harmonise enforcement against users who flout the rules on usage of pedestrian paths, footpaths and shared paths, thereby endangering other users; particularly pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the ambit of "path connected open spaces".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the proposed Bill, is it still the intention exclude both areas?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Void decks and frontage abutting commercial premises are sometimes connected to paths as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it not be better to harmonise the application of the laws dealing with PMD users under one Act?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, and this is my final point, in bringing path connected open spaces under the AMA, how is it proposed that the areas are demarcated as pedestrian paths, footpaths or shared paths respectively.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me better to provide clear demarcation of areas where use of vehicles are permitted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will augment the harmonisation of usage of paths and areas amongst pedestrians and vehicle users.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Mr Speaker, Sir, I support these two latest Bills to further strengthen safety in the use of PMDs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are all concerned about the safety of PMDs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not only do they compromise the safety on shared paths, they also create fire risks when being charged.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, after a number of serious accidents involving PMDs occurred on footpaths, I asked for a temporary halt on PMD imports during a Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Requiring approvals from LTA is a necessary step.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, I will urge LTA to err on the safe side in the approval of the new devices as there will always be new and innovative devices that will be brought to the market; they may seem safe initially but develop unforeseen problems after some usage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should not take chances on fire safety.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Once the public has bought the devices and started using them, it would be very difficult to call back.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is there a need for the devices to undergo inspection after some years of usage to ascertain their safety worthiness?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides being the approving authority for new devices, LTA can also regulate the number of devices allowed, given our limited pathways.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Again, it is always better to be safe and conservative.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of the reasons why the public was concerned about PMDs last year was the sheer number and the high utilisation rate of these devices, increasing the likelihood of accidents.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I support the immediate forfeiture of the devices assessed to be dangerous.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The proposal to put in upstream measures to prevent unauthorised import of non-compliant small motorised vehicles is absolutely necessary.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These vehicles include personal mobility devices (PMDs) and power-assisted bicycles (PABs) which come in many configurations and specifications.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Very unfortunately, we have seen how, in the absence of import controls, how many of these devices had caused fires, resulting in injuries, loss of lives and property damage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, some of these devices can attain maximum speeds way in excess of what is permitted and the speed differentials with other users on footpaths had led to accidents and serious injuries.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the legislative framework in place, enforcement will be key.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share how it will monitor individuals who purchase online and import devices which may not be compliant with our regulations?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will MOT work with our Customs to check on these imports?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another challenge is how MOT will check on those who modify the PMDs and PABs themselves as well as workshops or retail shops that are involved in illegal modifications.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider recruiting volunteers who can be trained and deployed to assist enforcement officers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How about providing incentives or rewards to those who have assisted and given the necessary information regarding offenders?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that LTA has widened the enforcement area to include path-connected open spaces against the illegal PMD riders on these paths.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have greater clarity now that it is specifically stated that paved open spaces can only be accessed by pedestrians, personal mobility aid users, bicycles and non-motorised PMDs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, it is clear that connectivity is ensured for these groups of users, with their safety enhanced by keeping motorised PMDs, which can travel at higher speeds, out of these paths.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will promote responsible and sustainable usage of the paths for all.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we are encouraging a healthy way of transportation and reducing our carbon footprint while promoting active lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I welcome the move to let LTA will take over the enforcement of offences under the AMA from the Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last but not least, I seek clarification about the age of offenders that the law will apply to as quite a number of such offenders in the past have been teenagers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Especially on the weekends, power-assisted bicycles (PABs) and motorised personal mobility devices (PMDs) cruising along the park connectors are a common sight.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I expect that these small motorised vehicles will continue to be the favourable mode of transport in the current and post COVID-19 period, as people try to avoid taking public transport, while working some exercise and getting some fresh air into their new regimes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As Singaporeans turn to contactless delivery for their daily needs and wants, the number of trips taken and users of these vehicles will undoubtedly continue to rise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is, hence, very timely to address the concerns brought about by non-compliant devices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In densely-populated Singapore, this has a spillover effect to the neighbouring houses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wish to ask how enforcement will be implemented against online purchase of small motorised vehicles by individuals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: New innovations have made it possible to modify these vehicles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With some tools and online tutorials, one can even do it yourself at home.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While a strict import controls regime will help to prevent innocent consumers from being misled into purchasing poor quality non-compliant products, there still remains individuals and businesses who have the capabilities to illegally modify a once-compliant product.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister share the challenges of apprehending such errant businesses and individuals and what is being done to mitigate them?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe heavier penalties and education would be a big part of the solution.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope LTA will make a public list available for easy viewing that clearly defines what is illegal and dangerous and to update a list of approved vehicles and parts on a regular basis to stay abreast with the ever-changing technology and innovations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am concerned that the extra cost will be passed on to consumers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Lastly, on a positive note, I am pleased to observe that the circuit breaker has brought out the sporty side of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite social distancing measures, Singaporeans have found ways to keep fit alone, from following online fitness videos at home to working out, jogging and cycling near their homes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As flexible work-from-home arrangements persist after the circuit breaker, I believe Singaporeans will continue to persevere with these endeavours to keep fit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Cycling is truly a great activity for both families and individuals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also a useful mode of transportation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Currently, most power-assisted bikes or bicylces on the list of Approved PABs are generally for city use.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Ministry look into other ranges, like electric mountain bikes, which is a new innovation – you can mountain bikes fitted with electric powered trains that can run mountain bikes on trails – to cater to sports enthusiasts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, whether this covers this range of products in the future would be useful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the circuit breaker comes to an end soon, slightly more people will start moving about in the community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us hope riders and users will not forget to comply with the rules on safe riding on footpaths and roads.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, I urge the Ministry to consider requiring cyclists and non-motorised PMD users to dismount and push their devices when they approach areas with fitness equipment, hardcourts or playgrounds as there are children running around and the elderly using the fitness equipment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most usually dismount or even avoid these areas, but for those who do not, it would be dangerous.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are a few playgrounds in my constituency in Henderson Dawson where there are little house-like structures that children love to play in.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because the children love to play hide-and-seek there with one another.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, it is dangerous when a child suddenly runs out of this "home", and onto the path of a rider.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As for elderly, their reflexes might be slower, and if there is an oncoming rider, they may not be able to move out of its path in time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is because at these locations, there are always children running around and the elderly people walking nearby to use the exercise equipment, and accidents easily happen.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my constituency, there are a few playgrounds with little houses and children love playing hide-and-seek there.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the kids suddenly run out of the small houses and dash onto the adjacent paths, they could be knocked down by the bicycles or PMDs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As for the elderly, their reflexes may be slower and if there are riders approaching, they may not be able to move away in time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important to explain the different aspects clearly and carefully so that all users know how to share the usage of paths responsibly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The public education programme should be continuous so that every cohort of riders and pedestrians is taught and reminded of the necessary etiquette on pathways.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is how we can maintain a safe environment for active mobility in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The present proposed Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Bill is meant to further enhance the safety of PMD and PAB users by ensuring that the devices imported into Singapore meet the required safety standards.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In one of the worst cases, a homeowner died in hospital two days after he was rescued from a burning flat where the blaze was linked to three burnt e-scooters.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And just recently on 20 May, three residents were taken to hospital due to a PAB fire.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not only do these fires impact the immediate users and family members of PMD/PAB users, they also affect the rest of the residents in the surrounding units as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Bill is thus proposed with the view that we need to better safeguard the lives and property of PMD/PAB users by ensuring that these devices are safe for use and do not pose a threat to the users and those around them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Part 2, clauses 5 to 8 of the Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Bill lays out the conditions regarding the import of small motorised vehicles and Part 3, clauses 9 to 15 of the Bill lays out the enforcement conditions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, will the Bill restrict individuals from purchasing non-compliant PMD/PAB from online retailers who are located overseas and then bringing in these vehicles for their own personal use?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, how would the Bill be applied to individuals who import or buy such vehicles online for their family members?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A casual search on online platforms, such as Carousell, reveals that there are many individuals who are reselling PMDs and PABs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I do not have exact figures, Mr Speaker, Sir, it would be reasonable to assume that the present circuit breaker (CB) measures have resulted in an increase in online commercial activity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, it might be good for the Government to consider the Bill against the platform of online sales and "resales".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the same vein, Mr Speaker, the Active Mobility (Amendment No. 2) Bill complements the earlier Active Mobility (Amendment) Bill that was passed in Parliament this year to further enhance the safety of pedestrians by broadening the coverage of the original Bill to cover path-connected spaces to facilitate active mobility while also enhancing enforcement against active mobility violations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe these amendments will be welcomed by pedestrians, especially young families or the elderly who frequent neighbourhood malls where some riders can often be seen riding across the open-air atriums of these malls to reach their destinations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have received feedback that examples of some areas where this has been happening with frequency are Buangkok Square, Punggol's Oasis Terrace and Westgate, just to name three.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, Mr Speaker, I believe that while these amendments to the Bill will provide an additional safeguard to the well-being of pedestrians, we also need to ensure that the policy does not eventually make existing users of PABs worse off, especially those individuals like food delivery riders who depend on PABs for their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Due to the recent amendments of the Bill, many food delivery riders who used to own PMDs have switched to PABs to complete their deliveries and they would, sometimes, ride into the atriums of the malls before dismounting from their PABs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the new proposed amendments to the Bill, adequate parking spaces for PABs must be provided nearby so that delivery riders can park their PABs safely and securely, without having to ride into the atrium of the mall or to find suitable parking spaces that might be some distance away.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That might also, of course, also impinge their mode of delivery.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other malls, such as Funan Mall and Westgate, that currently provide a thoroughfare for cyclists and PABs users, could possibly thus have to rethink how to design and designate the use of their thoroughfare in view of these amendments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Government may introduce Bills to prevent unauthorised entry of non-compliant devices, I would like to ask the Minister to clarify the Government's position is with regard to individuals or businesses who engage in the unauthorised modification of PMDs and PABs since these modifications are often one of the main causes of fire.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These PMDs/PABs might be compliant with standards when they were first imported but then eventually became "non-compliant" over time due to modifications that could eventually endanger the lives of users and others around them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, there was a resident in my constituency who actually ran an informal PAB/PMD modification workshop from his HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, notwithstanding my clarifications, I conclude my speech in firm support of both Bills.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I am glad that many Members spoke up in support of the import controls regime, which will complement existing regulations on retailers against the display, advertisement and sale of non-compliant devices, and regulations on end users against the use of non-compliant devices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Darryl David, Mr Dennis Tan, Mr Melvin Yong, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira and Mr Gan Thiam Poh had asked whether the coverage of the regime would be sufficiently wide, and some have suggested that we go even further to stem an inflow of unauthorised devices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will apply regardless of who imports them, whether by a wholesaler or retailer to sell, or by an individual buying via an online platform, and regardless of the purpose for which the device is imported.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Members of Parliament have raised a range of views on whether to regulate the import of spare parts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While the Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Bill does not cover the import of spare parts, some Members of Parliament have called for this to be regulated, since such parts may be used to create non-compliant devices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Others have pointed out that this would inconvenience users who source for their own spare parts and affect competition in the market for repairs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA will continue to engage and work with industry partners on the process as we implement the import control regime.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira raised concerns over whether the Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Bill would increase costs for businesses and consumers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will work to keep the import process simple and import approval and application fees low.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Details will be released at a later date.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To Mr Melvin Yong's query on whether the Bill will affect the Free Trade Agreements that Singapore has signed with other countries, MOT will administer the import control regime in a non-discriminatory and transparent manner, and is also working closely with MTI to ensure that Singapore continues to comply with our international trade obligations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira mentioned that the Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Bill would put in place an importer licensing regime.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To clarify, clause 5 of the Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Bill does not do this.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It simply requires any entity that imports devices to obtain import approval from LTA for each import transaction.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the moment, we do not have plans to license the importer as that could be an additional regulatory burden and may restrict competition, as Assoc Prof Walter Theseira has pointed out.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked why we took so long to put in place the import control regime.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOT and LTA have taken a calibrated approach in introducing device-related regulations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We had already put in place regulations that enforce against the sale, display, advertisement of non-compliant PMDs in 2017.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As the number of non-compliant devices being used on public paths remains significant and, after receiving feedback from Members of Parliament, including Mr Dennis Tan, we embarked on an extensive study of implementing import controls, bearing in mind that it has to be done so in accordance with our FTA obligations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As Mr Louis Ng had rightly pointed out, many of these devices may be dangerous and pose significant fire risks.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA has already put in place measures to mitigate these risks, including storing them in sheltered areas to avoid exposing them to harsh conditions, 24/7 monitoring of the holding yards, and installing fire extinguishers and sprinkler systems.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our proposal to shorten the forfeiture process for dangerous vehicles and things will enable LTA to better manage the risks from their prolonged storage.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The batteries are also dismantled and sold off to battery recyclers appointed by NEA.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Even as we seek to curb the risks arising from non-compliant vehicles, we have not lost sight of the importance of preserving the property rights of individuals to their devices and things, bearing in mind that as I have explained in my opening speech, there could be legitimate uses of non-compliant devices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Murali Pillai's concern on whether LTA is better placed to forfeit such vehicles or whether they should be left to the Courts to better safeguard individual property rights and due process, LTA will only seize and forfeit vehicles after LTA and relevant authorities have gathered supporting evidence and is reasonably certain that the vehicle was connected to the commission of an offence under the Active Mobility Act, Road Traffic Act or Small Motorised (Vehicles) Safety Bill.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The prosecution for cases involving the devices will remain independent of the forfeiture.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There were also questions about the device disposal process and LTA's powers to return devices before disposal.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This recognises that there may be legitimate claims to the seized vehicles.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For instance, an individual whose device was stolen might have a legitimate claim for the PMD to be returned to him since he may have obtained an import approval to bring in a non-compliant device for R&D purposes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While Members of Parliament have suggested that LTA should not return any non-compliant seized vehicles at all despite legitimate claims, this may unfairly undermine the property rights of vehicle owners.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: That said, vehicle owners should bear responsibility for assessing whether their devices are safe, and should safely dispose devices that may become dangerous.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As to Mr Louis Ng's other question on notifying the owner before disposal, let me clarify that the requirements for LTA to give notice to the owner of the vehicle, under sections 45 or 46 of the Active Mobility Act, continue to apply.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But let me assure Members that, where possible, LTA will reach out to the owner to notify them that their device is to be disposed of, on top of publication in the Gazette.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The public notice in the Gazette is necessary as there will be situations where LTA is not otherwise aware of the owner of the vehicle or thing.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA also publishes the disposal notice on its OneMotoring website to facilitate public awareness.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has rightly observed, this extension complements our other efforts to ensure public path safety.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Once these areas are public paths, all the other active mobility regulations, including speed limits, restrictions against reckless device usage, and the Code of Conduct, will apply.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The amendment in the Active Mobility (Amendment No. 2) Bill will thus ensure connectivity for path users, provide greater clarity and assurance to all path users, and promote responsible and sustainable usage of the paths for all.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To answer Mr Murali Pillai's and Mr Dennis Tan's queries, LTA will specify which path-connected open space is a pedestrian-only area, a footpath, or a shared path.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Most path-connected open spaces will be demarcated as footpaths, similar to the approach taken for paths today.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA will work with local stakeholders on this and steps will be taken to demarcate the different types of paths by markings or signboards if deemed necessary.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To answer Mr Murali Pillai's question, LTA and Town Councils had earlier evaluated that void decks and the frontage of commercial spaces (which are today excluded from the public path system) were not critical for active mobility connectivity and had safety concerns, such as numerous blind spots.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These spaces are currently regulated under Town Council by-laws.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As for Ms Joan Pereira's concern about certain areas, such as hard courts and playgrounds, LTA will work with the Town Councils to conduct ground enforcement and ensure safe device usage.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Town Councils could also consider whether erecting physical barriers around playgrounds would be appropriate for keeping children out of harm's way.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will also keep up our education efforts to remind users to slow down when nearing areas with potential blind spots or which may be crowded, such as bus stops or playgrounds.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Many Members of Parliament have also taken the opportunity at this Second Reading of the two Bills to raise issues not directly concerned with either Bill, but on Active Mobility more generally.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With the permission of Mr Speaker, I will deal with these very briefly.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ultimately, as Mr Gan Thiam Poh has pointed out, the effectiveness of all our regulations boil down to enforcement.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA has a comprehensive regime that enforces against non-compliant devices at multiple touchpoints, beyond registration and inspection.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA has significantly grown its enforcement footprint to about 200 enforcement officers, allowing for more frequent patrols.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA also works closely with enforcement officers across various agencies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To augment LTA's enforcement efforts, I agree with Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah that we should enlist the aid of technology and the wider community.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The "Report PMD/PAB Incident" function on the MyTransport.SG app also allows eye witnesses to report instances of errant behaviour.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As Mr Gan Thiam Poh has suggested, LTA has recruited Active Mobility Patrol volunteers to engage residents on active mobility rules and regulations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This limits the circulation of non-compliant devices and reduces the likelihood that consumers purchase them inadvertently.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA passed amendments earlier this year to significantly increase the penalties for retailer offences and will require all retailers to send in their e-scooters for inspections before sale.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also require e-scooters to undergo regular inspections to ensure device safety and deter against illegal modification.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA also monitors feedback relating to illegal modification of devices closely and conducts regularly checks on workshops and retailers to ensure compliance.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To answer Mr Gan Thiam Poh’s question about young offenders, the provisions in these current Bills do not stipulate a minimum age, but our Courts retain discretion to consider the circumstances of the case, including the age of the individual and the laws on sentencing of young offenders, in deciding the actual punishment to be meted out.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are also targeting younger riders in schools with our education efforts, such as the Safe Riding Programme, and like Mr Dennis Tan suggested, enhancing public education efforts, including reaching out through Active Mobility Patrol volunteers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Active Mobility Advisory Panel (AMAP) has joined us in emphasising the importance of public education and engagement by designating this as a focus for their current term.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: AMAP and LTA are already working with the insurance industry to study the risk pool, design and structure of individual insurance options.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the meantime, we strongly encourage individual active mobility device riders to purchase third-party liability insurance for their own protection against third-party claims.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since May 2019, we have stepped up the level of active mobility enforcement consistently in view of rising public path safety concerns.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I assure Er Dr Lee Bee Wah that even during the circuit breaker period, LTA has continued to mount regular active mobility enforcement operations to enforce against errant riders.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It has been challenging for our enforcement officers to balance all aspects of their enforcement duties with their concurrent responsibilities to enforce against breaches of safe distancing measures.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With the necessary infrastructure and regulatory regime, I am optimistic that active mobility will be more widely adopted.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Melvin Yong and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira have noted, the active mobility landscape will continue to evolve.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA will remain open to including new devices types in its publicly available list of approved device models, or consider new device safety standards for use on paths and roads, provided they are suitable for our local context.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ensuring fire and device safety is the responsibility of every device user – it is necessary to protect riders themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah had expressed concern over a recent fire incident in Yishun.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Even as we tighten our regulatory regimes at different levels, let me take this opportunity to remind all device users to practise safe charging habits.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Devices should not be left charging without monitoring, or overnight.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Users should not modify the electrical systems of their devices and should only use original power adaptors and approved battery models for that vehicle type.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA is working with SCDF to strengthen educational campaigns and outreach programmes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I concur with Mr Liang Eng Hwa that we should strive to ensure that infrastructure is more than adequate for the active mobility device population.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Liang also asked if we should set an effective life span for approved PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To Mr Dennis Tan's query, we had planned for eight in 10 HDB households to be minutes away from the expanded cycling path network by 2026, where PMD riders will only need to push their PMDs for a short distance.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will put us on a more sustainable trajectory, as active mobility adoption continues to increase.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: (In Mandarin):   	Mr Speaker, we remain committed to ensuring a safe active mobility landscape, especially with regard to path and fire safety.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Bills today help to ensure that devices are safe by controlling their import into Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They also allow LTA to shorten the forfeiture process for devices that pose significant safety risks, and expand the public path network to include certain open spaces, so that active mobility devices can be used safely in accordance with our regulations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Even as we tighten our regulatory regime at different levels, all device users need to use original power adaptors and approved battery models for that vehicle type.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Do not be careless and leave devices charging overnight without monitoring.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Government will strive to ensure that infrastructure is more than adequate for the active mobility device population.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We plan to expand the cycling path network by 2026.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Then, eight in 10 HDB households will be minutes away from the expanded cycling path network.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If our plans come to fruition, LTA will also expand the cycling path network to 1,320 km by 2030.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: (In English): We have come a long way in our journey on the active mobility front.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We may not have had all the answers right from the beginning, but I am thankful for the guidance, the feedback and support Members of this House have given me and my predecessors over the years.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To quote Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, one of our greatest advocates for PMDs safety, "Everyone has a shared responsibility for staying safe in their environment." Indeed, the Government cannot do this alone.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We need the collective effort of everyone – the active mobility users, the retailers, the pedestrians and other road users.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue with our efforts to work towards a safer, more sustainable active mobility landscape.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Let us all stay safe together, active together, SG Together.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I beg to move.
